t.2.46.1: When the night had brightened into dawn, the broad-chested and greatly renowned Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, who bore auspicious marks.
t.2.46.2: This is the hour of sunrise; the blessed night has passed. Listen, dear friend, that jet-black bird, the cuckoo, is calling.
t.2.46.3: The cry of peacocks calling in the forest is heard. Gentle one, let us cross the swift-flowing Jāhnavī, which goes to the ocean.
t.2.46.4: Having understood Rāma's words, Saumitri, the delight of his friends, took leave of Guha and the charioteer and stood before his brother.
t.2.46.5: Then, having fastened on their quivers and girded on their swords, the two Rāghavas, bearing their bows, set out with Sītā along the way that led to the Gaṅgā.
t.2.46.6: Approaching Rāma himself, the knower of dharma, in a humble manner, the charioteer, with joined palms, said: "What shall I do?"
t.2.46.7: He said to him, "Turn back, for this much has been done for me; leaving the chariot behind, we shall go on foot into the great forest."
t.2.46.8: But seeing that he himself had been given leave to go, the charioteer Sumantra, distressed, spoke these words to the Aikṣvāka, that tiger among men.
t.2.46.9: Never before in this world has any man had to undergo such a thing as this: your dwelling in the forest like a common man, together with your brother and your wife.
t.2.46.10: I do not think there is any yield of fruit in celibate discipline, in the study of the Veda, or even in gentleness and uprightness, if you have fallen into such misfortune.
t.2.46.11: O Rāghava, O hero, dwelling in the forest together with Vaidehī and your brother, you will attain the highest goal, as though conquering the three worlds.
t.2.46.12: We are surely ruined, O Rāma, we who have been deceived by her as well; sharers in sorrow, we shall fall under the power of the wicked Kaikeyī.
t.2.46.13: Speaking thus, the charioteer Sumantra, seeing Rāma, who was dear to him as his own self, gone far away, wept for a long time, stricken with grief.
t.2.46.15: I do not see any friend of the Ikṣvākus equal to you; act in such a way that King Daśaratha does not grieve for me.
t.2.46.14: Then, when the tears had ceased, Rāma spoke sweet words again and again to the charioteer, who had touched water and was pure.
t.2.46.16: The lord of the earth is old, his mind is stricken with grief, and he is sinking under the burden of desire; therefore I say this to you.
t.2.46.17: Whatever that great-souled lord of the earth may command, for the sake of fulfilling the wishes dear to Kaikeyī, that must be done without hesitation.
t.2.46.18: For it is for this very purpose that lords of men rule their kingdoms, that their will may not be thwarted in any of their undertakings.
t.2.46.19: So act, Sumantra, that the great king does not fall into falsehood and is not tormented by grief.
t.2.46.20: Having first saluted the king, who is aged, noble, master of his senses, and has never before known sorrow, you should speak these words to him on my behalf.
t.2.46.21: Neither I nor Lakṣmaṇa nor Maithilī grieve at the thought that we have been cast out of Ayodhyā, or that we shall dwell in the forest.
t.2.46.22: When the fourteen years have run their course, you will see Lakṣmaṇa, me, and Sītā swiftly returned, again and again.
t.2.46.23: Having spoken thus, O Sumantra, to the king and to my mother, to the other queens gathered together, and to Kaikeyī, again and again…
t.2.46.24: Tell Kausalyā that we are well, and then, in the words of Sītā, of me, and of the noble Lakṣmaṇa, offer her our salutations at her feet.
t.2.46.25: And you should say to the great king: “Bring Bharata here quickly, and once Bharata has arrived, let him be installed in the position the king has approved.”
t.2.46.27: And Bharata too must be told: "Just as you conduct yourself toward the king, so should you conduct yourself toward all the mothers, without any distinction."
t.2.46.26: Once you have embraced Bharata and consecrated him as heir apparent, the sorrow born of your anguish over us will not overpower you.
t.2.46.29: Being sent back by Rāma, Sumantra, worn down by grief, heard all those words and, out of affection, spoke to Kākutstha.
t.2.46.28: Just as Kaikeyī and Sumitrā are yours without distinction, so too is Queen Kausalyā, my mother, and especially so.
t.2.46.30: Whatever I may say without due courtesy, speaking out of affection and without faltering, because I am devoted to you, those words you ought to forgive.
t.2.46.31: How indeed shall I, bereft of you, return to that city, which, dear one, through separation from you is as though distraught with grief for a lost son?
t.2.46.32: When the people saw my chariot even with Rāma in it, they were stricken with grief; seeing the chariot without Rāma, that city may well break apart.
t.2.46.33: For the city would sink into despair on seeing this empty chariot, as if seeing its own army with only the charioteer left and its hero slain in battle.
t.2.46.34: Though you dwell far away, the people, thinking of you today as standing before them in their minds, have surely been made to go without food.
t.2.46.35: For the cry of anguish that the citizens raised at his banishment, they would then make a hundredfold louder the moment they saw me standing in the chariot.
t.2.46.36: And what indeed shall I say to the queen? 'Your son has been taken by me to his maternal uncle's house; do not grieve'?
t.2.46.37: I would not speak such words even if they were untrue; how then could I speak this unwelcome speech, which is true?
t.2.46.38: These finest of horses, who obey my command and carry your kinsfolk, how will they draw the chariot when it is bereft of you?
t.2.46.39: If, even as I plead with you, you insist on abandoning me, then the moment I am forsaken here by you, I shall enter the fire together with my chariot.
t.2.46.40: Whatever creatures in the forest may hinder your austerities, I shall drive them away with my chariot, O Rāghava.
t.2.46.41: On your account I have not gained the happiness that comes from driving the chariot; yet through you I hope to gain the happiness that comes from dwelling in the forest.
t.2.46.42: Be gracious: I wish to be your close companion in the forest. I long to hear you say with affection, 'Be close beside me, your master.'
t.2.46.44: For without you I cannot enter that Ayodhyā, just as one whose deeds are wicked cannot enter the royal city of great Indra.
t.2.46.43: Living in the forest, I will serve you with bowed head; I give up Ayodhyā, or even the world of the gods, entirely.
t.2.46.45: And these horses too, O hero, if they, dwelling in the forest, render service, will attain the highest state.
t.2.46.46: For this is my heart's desire: that when the term of your forest-dwelling has come to its end, I may carry you back to the city once more in this very chariot.
t.2.46.47: For if I am with you in the forest, the fourteen years will pass like a moment; but otherwise they will pass as though they were hundreds.
t.2.46.48: O you who are affectionate toward your servants, you ought not to abandon me, a devoted servant who stands on the path taken by my master's son and remains steadfast within the bounds of duty.
t.2.46.49: But Rāma, compassionate toward his servants, spoke these words to Sumantra, who was thus pleading again and again, piteously and in many ways.
t.2.46.50: I know your supreme devotion to me, O you who are loving toward your master. Now hear also the reason for which I am sending you from here back to the city.
t.2.46.51: Seeing you return to the city, my younger mother Kaikeyī may be convinced that Rāma has gone to the forest.
t.2.46.52: For that queen, fully satisfied once I have gone to dwell in the forest, would no longer suspect the righteous king of being a speaker of falsehood.
t.2.46.54: For my sake and for the king's, return to the city with the chariot, and whatever matters you have been charged with, report each of them exactly as they were told to you.
t.2.46.55: Having spoken these words to the charioteer and comforted him again and again, Rāma spoke to Guha words that were resolute and full of reason: "I shall go only after making my hair into matted locks; bring me the milky sap of the banyan tree."
t.2.46.53: This is my first wish: that my younger mother may obtain the prosperous kingdom for her son, protected by Bharata.
t.2.46.56: Guha quickly brought that milky sap to the prince, and with it Rāma fashioned matted locks for Lakṣmaṇa and for himself.
t.2.46.57: Then the two brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, clad in bark garments and wearing their matted hair coiled in a crown, shone forth like seers.
t.2.46.58: Then Rāma, who together with Lakṣmaṇa had taken up the path of the Vaikhānasa hermits and had undertaken the vow, spoke to Guha, his companion.
t.2.46.59: O Guha, be vigilant in regard to your army, your treasury, your fortress and likewise your realm, for a kingdom is held to be the hardest of all things to guard.
t.2.46.60: Then, having taken leave of Guha, the delight of the Ikṣvākus went on swiftly and undisturbed, together with his wife and with Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.46.61: But the delight of the Ikṣvākus, wishing to cross the swift-flowing Gaṅgā, saw a boat on the riverbank and spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.46.62: Tiger among men, slowly board this boat that stands ready here, and, taking hold of the high-minded Sītā, help her aboard right after you.
t.2.46.63: Hearing his brother's command and opposing none of it, he first helped Maithilī aboard, and then the self-possessed one climbed in himself.
t.2.46.64: Then the radiant elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa himself climbed aboard. Thereupon Guha, the lord of the Niṣādas, urged on his kinsmen.
t.2.46.65: Having taken leave of Sumantra and of Guha together with his host, Rāma boarded the boat and urged the boatmen on.
t.2.46.66: Then that boat, urged on by them and steadied by the helmsman, driven by the swift strokes of fine oars, quickly crossed the water.
t.2.46.67: Having reached the middle of the Bhāgīrathī, the blameless Vaidehī, joining her palms in reverence, spoke these words to that river.
t.2.46.68: This is the son of the wise great king Daśaratha; O Gaṅgā, protected by you, may he carry out this command.
t.2.46.70: Then, O fortunate goddess Gaṅgā, having returned again in safety, I shall joyfully worship you for the fulfillment of all desires.
t.2.46.71: For you, O goddess, flowing along three paths, behold the world of Brahmā, and in this world you are seen as the wife of the king of the ocean.
t.2.46.69: For after dwelling in the forest for fourteen full years, he will return once more, together with his brother and with me.
t.2.46.72: O goddess, O lovely one, I bow to you and sing your praise, for when that tiger among men has returned again in safety, the kingdom will be his once more.
t.2.46.73: Out of a desire to please you, I shall give hundreds of thousands of cows, garments, and fine food to the brāhmaṇas.
t.2.46.75: Having reached the far bank and left the boat behind, that bull among men, the scorcher of foes, set out together with his brother and with Vaidehī.
t.2.46.74: Speaking thus to the Gaṅgā, the blameless Sītā, moving southward, quickly reached the southern bank.
t.2.46.76: Then the mighty-armed one said to him who increased the joy of Sumitrā: "Go ahead, O Saumitri, and let Sītā follow you."
t.2.46.77: I shall walk behind, guarding both you and Sītā. But today Vaidehī will come to know the hardship of dwelling in the forest.
t.2.46.79: There the two of them killed four great beasts, a boar, an ṛśya antelope, a spotted deer and a great ruru deer, and, being hungry, quickly took the pure meat and at evening went to a great tree to spend the night.
t.2.46.78: Sumantra gazed long and steadily at Rāma, who had swiftly gone over to the far bank of the Gaṅgā. Then, his sight drawn back by the great distance, the wretched man, stricken with grief, shed tears.
